response.text:
Short answer you can say at lunch
- "Scanned PDF" = basically a picture of each page (no real text to select/search).  
- "Searchable PDF" = the file contains real text the viewer/indexer can find and copy — either because it was created from a text document (born-digital) or because OCR added a hidden text layer on top of scanned pages.

More detail (concise)

1. What’s actually inside
- Scanned / image-only PDF: each page is embedded as a raster image (JPEG/PNG-like). The PDF’s content stream just places the image; there are no text objects (no words, fonts, glyphs).  
- Searchable PDF (born-digital): the PDF stores text objects and font information. The characters are real PDF text, so viewers can highlight, copy, and font metrics are preserved.  
- Searchable PDF (OCRed): the PDF still contains page images (so it looks the same), but an extra invisible text layer was added (from OCR). That layer contains words and coordinates so the file becomes searchable/selectable.

2. How to tell which you have (quick checks)
- Try to select text with the mouse or press Ctrl/Cmd+F and search for a word. If neither works, it’s likely image-only.  
- Export or extract text (e.g., pdftotext). If output is empty or only gibberish, it’s probably image-only.  
- In Acrobat Reader, look for “Recognized text” / “OCR” notes or try Accessibility → Read Out Loud; tagged/recognized text will work.

3. Practical consequences
- Search/indexing: searchable PDFs can be indexed by search tools; image-only cannot.  
- Copy/paste & editing: only searchable PDFs allow accurate copy/paste and programmatic text extraction (OCR results may have errors).  
- Accessibility: screen readers need real text (and ideally tags). Searchable doesn’t guarantee full accessibility — tags/structure matter too.  
- File size/quality: scanned images can be large; OCR doesn’t necessarily reduce size and can introduce recognition errors.

One-line explanation for your coworker
- “A scanned PDF is just pictures of pages; a searchable PDF contains real text (either originally embedded or added by OCR), so you can search, select, and copy words.”
